input:
Sampling an effluent stream may sound like a simple, everyday task, but in practice it is absolutely essential to go about it in the right way, because the results obtained in the laboratory can only ever be as meaningful as the sample that was collected in the first place. A well-designed sampling procedure ensures that the sample genuinely represents the effluent as a whole, rather than merely capturing whatever happened to be passing at a particular moment.

First and foremost, the location at which samples are taken is of critical importance. Samples should be collected at a point where the effluent stream is thoroughly mixed and flowing steadily, such as at the outlet of a discharge pipe or just downstream of a weir, where the liquid has been turned over and its composition is uniform throughout. By contrast, dipping a container at the edge of a slow-moving channel, at the surface, or in a quiet corner where liquid sits almost still will only ever recover the liquid that happens to rest there, which may differ considerably from the effluent that the plant is actually discharging.

Equally important is the way in which increments are gathered and combined. Rather than relying on a single container filled at a single moment, a number of increments should be drawn at intervals spread across the whole of the discharge period under consideration, and these increments should then be combined, in proportion to the flow at the time each was drawn, to form one composite sample for analysis. This approach smooths out short-lived fluctuations and produces a sample that reflects the average composition of the discharge over the period as a whole.

The single grab sample, by comparison, is deeply misleading. The composition of an effluent stream changes continually throughout a shift as batches are emptied, vessels are washed down, and production rises and falls, so a sample captured at just one instant records whichever of those conditions happened to be passing at that moment. The result is then all too easily read as though it described the entire stream, painting a picture that is inaccurate and potentially costly in its consequences.
target:
A representative sample of an effluent stream is built, not taken. The sample that reaches the laboratory must stand for the whole discharge, and a composite sample assembled from increments drawn across the discharge period does this; a single grab sample does not.

Take the increments where the stream is mixed. The sampling point belongs where the flow is turbulent and the composition uniform across the stream: at the outlet of a discharge pipe, or downstream of a weir, where the liquid has just been turned over. A point at the bank of a slow channel, at the surface, or in a stagnant corner returns the liquid that happens to rest there, and that liquid is not the effluent the plant discharges.

Draw each increment at intervals spread over the period the sample has to cover, and combine the increments in proportion to the flow at the time each was drawn. The combined volume is the sample. Analysis then reports the composition of the discharge averaged over the period, weighted as the discharge itself was weighted.

The composite must also be handled as a sample in its own right. The combined increments are mixed before any portion is taken for analysis; a portion dipped from the top of an unmixed composite repeats the grab-sample error at a smaller scale, because the increments were drawn at different states of the stream and settle or separate while they stand. The record that travels with the sample states the period the sample covers and when each increment was drawn, so the laboratory result can be read against the discharge it claims to describe.

A grab sample fails on timing alone. Effluent composition changes through a shift as batches are emptied, vessels are washed down, and flows rise and fall. One container filled at one moment catches whichever of those states was passing, and the result is then read as if it described the whole stream. The analysis is not at fault; the sample was never the stream.
